Elegant ggplot2 (Arranging Plots), with tidyplots equivalents

Source: elegant_ggplot2_vs_tidyplot_9.qmd

Author

Steve Rozen (sr110@duke.edu, steverozen@pm.me)

Published

2026-06-28 20:07

About this handout

This follows the Arranging plots chapter of Hadley Wickham, Danielle Navarro, and Thomas Lin Pedersen’s ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis (3rd edition). For each step we keep the original ggplot2 + patchwork code, then show the tidyplots equivalent.

The headline is different from the other handouts in this series. The earlier chapters were about drawing one plot, where ggplot2 and tidyplots are two competing grammars. Arranging several finished plots into one figure is not part of either grammar. It is the job of a third package, patchwork, and the good news is:

  • patchwork operates on tidyplots objects unchanged. A tidyplot() returns an object that is still a ggplot under the hood, so +, /, |, plot_layout(), plot_annotation(), and inset_element() all work on tidyplots exactly as they do on ggplots.
  • So the translation in this chapter is almost a no-op: build each panel with whichever grammar you like, then compose them with the same patchwork code. The only thing that changes is how each individual panel is drawn.

Two things are worth naming up front because they are tidyplots-specific:

  1. tidyplots has no arranging grammar of its own. Its only multi-panel verb is split_plot(), which splits one plot into facet-like panels by a grouping variable. It does not compose distinct, separately-built plots. For that, you reach for patchwork.
  2. Always build tidyplots panels with width = NA, height = NA. tidyplots otherwise locks every panel to a fixed 50 x 50 mm square, which fights patchwork’s alignment and leaves panels different sizes. width = NA, height = NA lets each panel flex so patchwork can align and size them like ggplots.

Setup

library(ggplot2)        # the book's package
library(tidyplots)      # the package we translate each panel into
library(patchwork)      # the arranging package (works on BOTH)
library(dplyr)          # for the one mutate() precompute
data("mpg", package = "ggplot2")          # 234 car models

The four base plots

The chapter builds four example plots and then arranges them every which way. Here they are in both grammars. Notice that the arranging code later is identical; only these four definitions differ.

ggplot2

p1 <- ggplot(mpg) +
  geom_point(aes(x = displ, y = hwy))

p2 <- ggplot(mpg) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = as.character(year), fill = drv), position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = "year")

p3 <- ggplot(mpg) +
  geom_density(aes(x = hwy, fill = drv), colour = NA) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(drv))

p4 <- ggplot(mpg) +
  stat_summary(aes(x = drv, y = hwy, fill = drv), geom = "col", fun.data = mean_se) +
  stat_summary(aes(x = drv, y = hwy), geom = "errorbar", fun.data = mean_se, width = 0.5)

p1 + p2 + p3 + p4

tidyplots

The same four panels as tidyplots. Each carries width = NA, height = NA so patchwork can align them.

  • p2 (dodged count bar) becomes add_count_bar(). The color = drv mapping set in tidyplot() dodges the bars automatically.
  • p3 (filled density) has no native tidyplots verb, so it uses the escape hatch add(ggplot2::geom_density()) plus add(ggplot2::facet_grid()).
  • p4 (mean +/- SEM column) becomes add_mean_bar() then add_sem_errorbar(), two verbs instead of two stat_summary() layers.
mpg2 <- mpg |> mutate(year_chr = as.character(year))   # tidyplot() wants a bare column

t1 <- mpg |> tidyplot(x = displ, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points()

t2 <- mpg2 |> tidyplot(x = year_chr, color = drv, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_count_bar()

t3 <- mpg |> tidyplot(x = hwy, color = drv, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add(ggplot2::geom_density(ggplot2::aes(fill = drv), colour = NA)) |>
  add(ggplot2::facet_grid(rows = vars(drv)))

t4 <- mpg |> tidyplot(x = drv, y = hwy, color = drv, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_mean_bar() |>
  add_sem_errorbar()

t1 + t2 + t3 + t4     # <- identical patchwork code
NoteWhat to notice

The composition line t1 + t2 + t3 + t4 is byte-for-byte the same as p1 + p2 + p3 + p4. That is the whole point of this chapter: once a panel is built, patchwork does not care which grammar built it.

9.1 Laying out plots side by side

+ places plots next to each other and aligns their plotting regions. With no layout given, patchwork uses facet_wrap logic (four plots become a 2 x 2 grid, as above).

ggplot2

p1 + p2

tidyplots

t1 + t2

9.1.1 Taking control of the layout

Every operator below is pure patchwork, so the ggplot2 and tidyplots versions differ only in which letters (p vs t) name the panels.

plot_layout(ncol = ...)

  • ggplot2
  • tidyplots
p1 + p2 + p3 + plot_layout(ncol = 2)
t1 + t2 + t3 + plot_layout(ncol = 2)

Stacking and rows with / and |

/ stacks plots vertically, | places them in a row, and the two nest to build complex layouts.

  • ggplot2
  • tidyplots
p3 | (p2 / (p1 | p4))
t3 | (t2 / (t1 | t4))

Free-form layouts with a design string

A text block names where each plot goes. Letters are filled in plot order, # is empty space.

  • ggplot2
  • tidyplots
layout <- "
AAB
C#B
CDD
"

p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 + plot_layout(design = layout)
t1 + t2 + t3 + t4 + plot_layout(design = layout)

Collecting guides with guides = "collect"

guides = "collect" pulls duplicate legends out of the panels and shows one shared legend.

  • ggplot2
  • tidyplots
p2 + p4 + plot_layout(ncol = 2, guides = "collect")
t2 + t4 + plot_layout(ncol = 2, guides = "collect")
Warningtidyplots gotcha: collection only merges identical legends

patchwork merges two legends only when they are the same aesthetic with the same scale and title. In tidyplots the single color = argument maps to different underlying aesthetics depending on the geom (bar fill, boxplot outline, point colour). Two panels that both look “coloured by drv” can therefore produce two separate legends that will not collapse. t2 and t4 both use color = drv as a fill, so they collect into one legend. Mixing a filled bar with an outline-coloured boxplot would leave two. If a collected legend refuses to merge, check that every panel maps color to the same kind of geom.

A guide_area() reserves a slot in the layout for the collected legend:

  • ggplot2
  • tidyplots
p2 + p4 + guide_area() + plot_layout(ncol = 2, guides = "collect")
t2 + t4 + guide_area() + plot_layout(ncol = 2, guides = "collect")

9.1.2 Modifying subplots

A patchwork is still indexable. [[i]] reaches in to restyle one panel, and & applies a component to all panels at once.

Restyle one panel with [[ ]]

  • ggplot2
  • tidyplots
p12 <- p1 + p2
p12[[2]] <- p12[[2]] + theme_light()   # restyle only the second panel
p12
t12 <- t1 + t2
t12[[2]] <- t12[[2]] + theme_light()   # restyle only the second panel
t12

Apply to all panels with &

  • ggplot2
  • tidyplots
p1 + p4 & theme_minimal()
t1 + t4 & theme_minimal()
Warningtidyplots gotcha: & overwrites the tidyplots theme

& adds the component to every panel. Adding a complete ggplot2 theme such as theme_minimal() therefore replaces the tidyplots default styling on each panel (axis lines become a grid, the type face changes). That is fine when you want a uniform look, but if you wanted to keep the tidyplots appearance, use a narrower component (for example & scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 45))) instead of a whole theme.

A shared scale across panels is the safe use of &:

  • ggplot2
  • tidyplots
p1 + p4 & scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 45))
t1 + t4 & scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 45))

9.1.3 Adding annotation

plot_annotation() adds a title or caption for the whole assembly, and tag_levels auto-labels the panels.

Title and caption

  • ggplot2
  • tidyplots
p34 <- p3 + p4 + plot_annotation(
  title   = "A closer look at the effect of drive train in cars",
  caption = "Source: mpg dataset in ggplot2"
)
p34
t34 <- t3 + t4 + plot_annotation(
  title   = "A closer look at the effect of drive train in cars",
  caption = "Source: mpg dataset in ggplot2"
)
t34

Auto-tagging panels

  • ggplot2
  • tidyplots
p123 <- p1 | (p2 / p3)
p123 + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "I")
t123 <- t1 | (t2 / t3)
t123 + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "I")

9.2 Arranging plots on top of each other

inset_element() overlays one plot on another. Coordinates are normalized to the host panel (0 to 1). This is also pure patchwork and works on tidyplots panels.

  • ggplot2
  • tidyplots
p1 + inset_element(p2, left = 0.5, bottom = 0.45, right = 0.95, top = 0.95)
t1 + inset_element(t2, left = 0.5, bottom = 0.45, right = 0.95, top = 0.95)

A patchwork object can itself be the inset, and the inset can be tagged like any other panel:

  • ggplot2
  • tidyplots
p12_inset <- p1 + inset_element(p2, left = 0.5, bottom = 0.5, right = 0.9, top = 0.95)
p12_inset + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
t12_inset <- t1 + inset_element(t2, left = 0.5, bottom = 0.5, right = 0.9, top = 0.95)
t12_inset + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

9.3 Wrapping up: split_plot is not patchwork

tidyplots’ one native multi-panel verb, split_plot(), splits a single plot into panels by a grouping variable. It is tidyplots’ answer to facet_wrap(), not to patchwork. Use it when one dataset should be broken out by a factor:

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = displ, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points() |>
  split_plot(by = drv)        # one plot, three panels by drv (NOT a composition)

The distinction in one line:

  • split_plot(by = v) takes one plot and one variable, makes one panel per level. It is faceting.
  • patchwork (+, /, |, inset_element) takes several already-built, unrelated plots and arranges them. It is composition.

For everything in this chapter you want the second one, and tidyplots panels drop straight into it.
